notes.title: What a Voice Agent Is — One Turn, End to End
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Agents introduction · LiveKit — Pipeline types · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/as_built.md §1–2 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_design.md §2

TL;DR

A voice agent is a loop that turns a person's speech into words, decides when they have finished, works out a reply, and speaks it back fast enough to feel like conversation. Every stage is streaming, so the design question is never "how long does a stage take" but "how much of it can overlap with the person still talking".

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: person speaksaudio to the agentwordsturn over?replyvoice backperson hears it

Recall

Prompt Answer
The ten stages, in order capture, carry, clean, detect, transcribe, endpoint, think, speak, yield, observe
Which stage decides the person finished? endpoint (the turn detector), not the STT and not the VAD
What does "yield" mean? the agent stops speaking when the person talks over it (barge-in)
Which stages run on every 20 ms audio frame? capture, carry, clean, detect
Why stream every stage? so later stages start before earlier ones finish
Draw one turn as a timeline: browser, agent, vendors shows speech in, words back, the endpoint wait, model, TTS, voice out, and barge-in

The idea

Without it: a request-response design (record, upload, transcribe, answer, synthesise, play) waits for each step to finish. Seconds of silence after every sentence; nobody keeps talking to that.

It does: splits the turn into stages that each work on a stream: audio frames, partial words, the first tokens of the reply, the first bytes of voice. Each stage starts on the previous stage's first output.

It costs: you now own timing. Something must decide when the person has finished before all the words are in, and something must stop the voice when the person talks over it. Those two decisions, not the models, are where most voice agents feel wrong.

How it works

Stage Does Typical home Note
capture mic to frames; echo, noise, gain on device browser audio for engineers
carry frames to the agent and back, over WebRTC through an SFU media server WebRTC for voice AI
clean remove noise and the agent's own voice agent process 03 Audio cleanup
detect is someone speaking in this frame? (VAD) agent process 04 Listening
transcribe sound to words, partial and final STT vendor 04 Listening
endpoint finished, or pausing to think? agent process 05 Turn-taking
think choose and phrase the reply model vendor + your code 06 Thinking
speak text to voice, first sentence first TTS vendor 07 Speaking
yield stop the voice when the person talks over it; resume on a false alarm agent process 05 Turn-taking
observe per-turn timings, quality, cost everywhere 09 Production

Three rules hold for every stage: stream (emit the first piece as soon as it exists), overlap (start on the previous stage's first piece), and one authority per decision (one component decides end of turn, one decides barge-in).

Knobs

Knob Default (as of Oct 2026) Raise it → Lower it →
Pipeline shape cascaded STT → model → TTS (LiveKit's default) speech-to-speech: lower latency, less control –
Endpoint wait per turn detector fewer cut-off answers faster replies, more interruptions of the person
How early the reply starts after the turn is committed preemptive: before commit, discard if they keep talking –
Barge-in sensitivity LiveKit: adaptive on Cloud, else VAD ignores coughs and "mm-hm" stops faster on real interruptions

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Product Rachel interviews a candidate in the browser as_built §1
Transport LiveKit Cloud; browser holds a 30-minute room-scoped token as_built §2 row 2
Agent process one per interview, cleans, detects, transcribes, decides, speaks as_built §1
Brain per turn rules pick the move, one model call phrases it as_built §2 row 8
Analysis while the person talks Assessor and Prober run on each final phrase as_built §2 row 9
End of speech → first audio p50 3 383 ms, p95 4 948 ms (43 calls, 30 days to 16 Oct 2026, callers in India) as_built §3

Deviation: the design keeps the model call off the hot path by generating the reply while the candidate speaks; the build still makes one call after the turn ends (utkarsh_architecture.md §2.1 vs as_built §3).

Measure it

  • Metric — end of speech → first audio heard, p50 and p95, per turn. Target p50 ≤ 450 ms, p95 ≤ 800 ms.
  • See it — LiveKit's per-turn e2e_latency, with end_of_turn_delay, llm_node_ttft and tts_node_ttfb beside it, on each chat message's metrics.
  • Bounded by — a scripted reply when the model is late, a backup voice when TTS fails, resume after a false interruption.

Pitfalls

Thinking of it as three API calls

  • Why it's tempting: the cascade is literally STT, model, TTS, and each has a client library.
  • Why it's wrong: the slowest part is usually the endpoint wait, which is none of the three; and the calls overlap, so their sum is not the latency.
  • Think instead: draw the turn as a timeline and ask which stage the person is waiting on at each moment.

Optimising the model first

  • Why it's tempting: model latency is the number vendors publish and compete on.
  • Why it's wrong: in our build the endpoint wait is ~2 s of a 3.4 s median turn; a faster model moves the smaller share.
  • Think instead: measure each stage's share of the turn, then pull the biggest lever.

Letting two components decide the end of a turn

  • Why it's tempting: the STT vendor ships endpointing and so does the agent framework; leaving both on seems safer.
  • Why it's wrong: they disagree, and the turn ends on whichever fires first, cutting answers off or committing twice.
  • Think instead: one authority per decision; we turn vendor endpointing off.

Connections

all stages — this note is the map; the latency budget puts milliseconds on it.

  • chooses between pipeline shapes — cascaded vs speech-to-speech.
  • imitates how people take turns — what "natural" means.
  • carried by WebRTC for voice AI — the wire.
  • Say it: Q5 · Q26

notes.title: The Latency Budget — End of Speech to First Audio
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_capacity.md Part A · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/as_built.md §3 · LiveKit — Data hooks (per-turn metrics) · LiveKit — Pipeline types

TL;DR

The one number a person feels is the gap between their last word and the agent's first sound. Budget it stage by stage, and count only what sits in series after the person stops: anything that overlaps their speech is free.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: last wordturn committedfirst sentencefirst byteheard

Recall

Prompt Answer
What is measured, from where to where? end of the person's speech → first agent audio heard
Which stages are on the critical path? endpoint wait, model first token, TTS first byte, network and jitter
Why isn't full transcription on it? interim words stream during speech; only the final tail is after
Why quote p95, not just p50? people remember the slow turns
LiveKit says what feels natural? under about one second end to end
Draw the budget as a stacked bar: design vs measured design ~530 ms with no model call; measured 3.4 s, endpoint ~2 s

The idea

Without it: each team tunes its own stage, every stage looks fine, and the turn still takes three seconds because nobody owns the sum.

It does: names every stage that runs after the person stops, gives each a millisecond allowance, and makes the total a product target with an owner.

It costs: honesty. A budget written before measurement is a guess; ours missed by 7× at p50 because two items (the endpoint wait and a model call) were budgeted at ~200 ms and 0 ms.

How it works

Rule Because
Only serial work counts a stage that ran during the person's speech has already finished
Every item has an owner vendor stages (endpoint model, TTS, network) can only be chosen, configured or moved
Budget p50 and p95 separately the tail is a vendor queue or a slow network, not the median doubled
A stage you can remove beats one you can speed up pre-generating the reply deletes the model line

Knobs

Knob Default (as of Oct 2026) Raise it → Lower it →
Endpoint minimum wait turn detector's own fewer cut-off answers, +ms per turn faster, more people cut off mid-thought
Model on the hot path one call after commit – pre-generate during speech: line goes to ~0
Region wherever the vendor is – media, STT, TTS and model near the caller: saves round trips
First TTS chunk size first sentence smoother prosody, later first byte earlier first byte, choppier sentence start

🔊 In our system

Stage Budget Measured p50 Status note
Endpoint wait 150–250 ms 2 067 ms (p95 3 640) 0.8 s minimum silence, up to 3.5 s on a thinking pause
STT delay inside the wait 404 ms –
Model first token 0 (pre-generated) 442 ms (p95 1 714) one call still on the hot path; median is the network from India
TTS first byte 300 ms 342 ms (p95 379) goldens the same week: 328–339 ms
SFU + network + jitter 60–120 ms inside the total –
Total ~530 ms typical, ~690 ms p95; target p50 ≤ 450, p95 ≤ 800 3 383 ms, p95 4 948 ms 43 calls, 30 days to 16 Oct 2026, callers in India

Budget from voice_pipeline_capacity.md Part A; measured from as_built §3.

Against a common industry reference (a talk slide shared 16 Oct 2026, source not stated; totals checked: 15 + 200 + 100 + 100 = 415 ms, typical 1.12–1.93 s):

Component Best case Typical Ours ( p50)
VAD 15–20 ms 20–30 ms ~1 ms per frame (not a turn cost)
STT 200–300 ms 400–600 ms 404 ms
LLM (first token) 100–200 ms 500–1 000 ms 442 ms
TTS (first byte) 100–150 ms 200–300 ms 342 ms
Total ~415 ms 1.1–2 s —
Endpoint wait (not on the slide) — — 2 067 ms
End of speech → first audio — — 3 383 ms

Our STT, model and TTS sit inside the slide's typical band. What the slide leaves out is the end-of-turn wait: VAD's 15–30 ms is frame detection, not the silence you choose to wait before replying. That missing line is most of our gap. Deviation: the design has no model call and a ~200 ms endpoint; those two lines are the whole gap. The levers, in order: tune the endpoint wait on recorded answers, pre-generate the reply, move everything in-region, add a second model provider for the tail.

Measure it

  • Metric — e2e_latency p50 and p95 per turn, alongside end_of_turn_delay, llm_node_ttft, tts_node_ttfb; target p50 ≤ 450 ms, p95 ≤ 800 ms.
  • See it — LiveKit puts these on each chat message's metrics (conversation_item_added); per-plugin events carry end_of_utterance_delay, ttft, ttfb. Log them per turn with the turn id.
  • Bounded by — per-stage deadlines: a late model gives way to a scripted line, a failed TTS to a backup voice.

Pitfalls

Adding up every stage's latency

  • Why it's tempting: a budget looks like a sum, and every stage has a latency.
  • Why it's wrong: STT, VAD and background analysis mostly run while the person is still speaking; adding them double-counts and hides the real serial path.
  • Think instead: draw the timeline from the last word and count only what sits after it.

Budgeting the endpoint as a model's inference time

  • Why it's tempting: the turn-detector model infers in ~50 ms, so the line looks small.
  • Why it's wrong: the wait is mostly deliberate silence before the model is even asked; ours is 0.8 s minimum by design and 2 s measured.
  • Think instead: budget the silence you choose to wait, plus inference, and tune it on real recordings.

Quoting only the median

  • Why it's tempting: p50 is stable and looks good in a demo.
  • Why it's wrong: our model's p95 is ~4× its p50 because of the vendor's queue; one slow turn in five ruins an interview.
  • Think instead: report p50 and p95 per stage and set the target on p95.

Connections

capture → … → endpoint → think → speak → observe — the budget is the observe stage's first job.

  • puts numbers on one turn, end to end.
  • shrinks with a speech-to-speech model — fewer serial stages.
  • sets its target from how people take turns — ~200 ms human gaps.
  • wire share owned by time to first token (networking).
  • Say it: Q1 · Q4 · Q31

notes.title: Pipeline Shapes — Cascaded, Turn-Based Realtime, Full-Duplex
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Pipeline types (read 16 Oct 2026) · LiveKit — Realtime models · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/media_transport/livekit_decision.md The LangGraph seam

TL;DR

Three ways to build the middle of a voice agent: a cascade of separate STT, model and TTS; a turn-based realtime model that hears speech and speaks back after the turn; or a full-duplex model that listens and talks at once. You trade control and auditability for latency and expressiveness, in that order.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · design time

Flow: need text you can audit?cascadedneed overlap and backchannels?full-duplexturn-based realtime

Recall

Prompt Answer
The three shapes cascaded STT→LLM→TTS, turn-based realtime, full-duplex realtime
What the cascade gives up prosody: the model never hears tone, only words
What realtime models give up text control: delayed transcripts, no exact scripted lines, one provider
Who decides turns in full-duplex? the model itself
Why most production agents stay cascaded audit, tool calling, swap any stage, say exact words
Draw the three shapes side by side, boxes and arrows cascade: 3 boxes in series; realtime: 1 box after the turn; duplex: 1 box, both directions at once

The idea

Without a choice: teams pick a realtime model for the demo latency, then discover they can't show what the agent heard, can't force an exact disclaimer, and can't switch provider.

It does: names the three shapes so the choice is made on what the product must control, not on a demo.

It costs: cascaded pays a serial stage per hop (streaming hides most of it); realtime pays in control and lock-in; full-duplex pays in control over turn-taking itself.

How it works

Cascaded Turn-based realtime Full-duplex realtime
How three models in series, each swappable one model, waits for the turn, answers in speech one model, decides when turns start and stop
Latency each hop adds; streaming hides most lower baseline, stages merged same as realtime, plus overlap
Hears tone no, words only yes yes
Transcript interim and final, immediate delayed delayed
Exact scripted lines (say()) yes not the same way not the same way
Tool calling mature works less mature
Turn-taking yours (VAD, turn detector) model's or yours model's
Lock-in low: swap any stage one provider one provider
Example (as of Oct 2026, per LiveKit) any STT + LLM + TTS plugin OpenAI Realtime API OpenAI GPT-Live

LiveKit calls the cascade "the default for most production agents" and says conversations feel natural under about one second end to end (Pipeline types, read 16 Oct 2026). A half-cascade also exists: a realtime model for understanding with a separate TTS for the voice, keeping control over what is said (LiveKit: modalities=["text"] on the realtime model plus a tts on the session, at the cost of running two models; Realtime models page, read 16 Oct 2026).

Knobs

Knob Default (as of Oct 2026) Raise it → Lower it →
Shape cascaded realtime: lower latency, expressive, less control –
Who owns turn detection your turn detector (cascade) the model's server-side detector –
Separate TTS with a realtime model off exact voice and lexicon control, one more hop –

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Shape cascaded: Deepgram Nova-3 → model → Deepgram Aura-2 as_built §2 rows 5, 8, 10
Why not realtime an interview must record exactly what the candidate said and what was asked, with scripted questions spoken word for word as_built §3 What already limits it; livekit_decision
The brain our own graph (rules pick the move, a model phrases it), not LiveKit's handoffs livekit_decision The LangGraph seam

Measure it

  • Metric — end of speech → first audio per shape on the same calls, plus what the shape must guarantee (transcript accuracy, scripted-line fidelity).
  • See it — in a cascade llm_node_ttft and tts_node_ttfb are separate per-turn fields; with a realtime model they are not populated and RealtimeModelMetrics.ttft is the first audio token.
  • Bounded by — keep the cascade's interfaces so one stage can be swapped for a realtime model without rewriting the agent.

Pitfalls

Choosing realtime for the demo latency

  • Why it's tempting: one model, fewer hops, and the voice sounds more alive.
  • Why it's wrong: you lose the immediate transcript and exact scripted speech; for an audited conversation (interview, healthcare, payments) those are requirements.
  • Think instead: list what the product must control first; choose realtime only if nothing on that list needs text.

Assuming the cascade is slow by nature

  • Why it's tempting: three hops look like three latencies added.
  • Why it's wrong: streaming overlaps the hops; in our build the cascade's model and TTS together are ~0.8 s of a 3.4 s turn, and the endpoint wait is the rest.
  • Think instead: fix the endpoint wait and the hot-path model call before blaming the shape.

Connections

… → endpoint → think → speak → … — the shape decides what "think" is.

  • changes the budget of the latency budget — realtime merges stages.
  • decides who imitates human turn-taking — your detector or the model.
  • sits inside one turn, end to end.
  • Say it: Q10

notes.title: Audio for Engineers — Samples, Frames, Codecs
notes.html:
References

RFC 6716 — Opus · RFC 7587 — Opus over RTP · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_design.md §3, App. B Transport & media

TL;DR

Audio is a stream of samples, cut into 20 ms frames, compressed with Opus on the wire and handed to models as 16 kHz mono PCM. Every per-frame stage (echo, noise, VAD) runs 50 times a second, so its cost is in microseconds, not milliseconds.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per frame

Flow: mic20 ms framesRTP over WebRTC48 kHz PCM16 kHz monoVAD and STT

Recall

Prompt Answer
Frames per second at 20 ms 50
One 20 ms frame of 16 kHz 16-bit mono 320 samples, 640 bytes
What sample rate do speech models want? 16 kHz mono; nothing gained above it for STT
Why Opus on the wire? 8–24× smaller than PCM (vs 16 and 48 kHz), built for speech, survives loss
Phone audio 8 kHz: half the bandwidth of 16 kHz, lower STT accuracy
Draw the format at each hop, mic to STT 48 kHz PCM → Opus/RTP → 48 kHz PCM → 16 kHz mono PCM

The idea

Without it: a team sends 48 kHz stereo PCM to a speech model "for quality", pays 3× the bytes for nothing, and can't explain why VAD sees 10 ms frames while the STT wants 20.

It does: fixes three numbers per hop (sample rate, channels, frame length) and one codec on the wire.

It costs: a resample and a decode in the agent per frame; both are cheap, but every format change is a place to get the rate wrong and hear "chipmunk" audio.

How it works

Computed (16-bit samples, mono):

Rate Where it's used 20 ms frame PCM bitrate
8 kHz telephone networks (SIP) 160 samples · 320 B 128 kbps
16 kHz speech models (STT, VAD) 320 samples · 640 B 256 kbps
48 kHz WebRTC capture and playout, Opus internal 960 samples · 1 920 B 768 kbps
Term One line
PCM raw samples, what models consume
Opus the WebRTC speech codec; 20 ms frames by default; ~32 kbps for voice is 80 B per frame
RTP the packet that carries one or more frames; the SFU forwards it without decoding
Jitter buffer holds a few frames so uneven arrival plays smoothly; adds tens of ms
Mono one channel; speech models gain nothing from stereo

Knobs

Knob Default (as of Oct 2026) Raise it → Lower it →
Rate sent to STT vendor-specific; 16 kHz is the common target more bytes, no accuracy gain above 16 kHz 8 kHz: phone quality, more misheard words
Opus frame length 20 ms fewer packets, more delay per frame lower delay, more packet overhead
Channels mono for speech stereo: double bytes, no gain –

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Capture browser getUserMedia, mono, AEC + NS + AGC on as_built §2 row 1
Wire Opus, parameters left to LiveKit design §3 (deliberately not restated)
To STT 16 kHz mono to Deepgram design §3: "nothing is gained above 16k"

Measure it

  • Metric — STT word error rate and term recall on the exact rate you send; a format change must not move them.
  • See it — log the sample rate and channel count where audio enters STT; play one stored frame back.
  • Bounded by — resample in one place, in the agent, so a wrong rate is one bug, not three.

Pitfalls

Sending higher-rate audio for better recognition

  • Why it's tempting: more samples sounds like more information.
  • Why it's wrong: speech models are trained on 16 kHz; above that you pay bytes and resampling for no accuracy.
  • Think instead: send 16 kHz mono and spend the effort on vocabulary and noise.

Testing only on browser audio, then taking phone calls

  • Why it's tempting: the pipeline works, and SIP is "just another participant".
  • Why it's wrong: 8 kHz telephone audio loses the high frequencies that separate many consonants; accuracy drops.
  • Think instead: re-run the recognition goldens on 8 kHz audio before opening a phone line.

Connections

capture → carry → clean → … — the formats every later stage inherits.

  • carried by WebRTC for voice AI — Opus over RTP.
  • chosen over WebSocket PCM streaming.
  • feeds every per-frame stage of the turn.

notes.title: How People Take Turns — Gaps, Pauses, Backchannels, Overlap
notes.html:
References

Stivers et al. 2009 — Universals and cultural variation in turn-taking (PNAS) · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/interview_prep/07-backchannel-overlap.md · LiveKit — Turn detection & interruptions

TL;DR

People hand the floor over in about 200 ms, which is faster than they can plan a reply, so listeners predict the end of a turn instead of waiting for silence. A voice agent can't predict as well, so it must tell four sounds apart: a pause (still their turn), an end (your turn), a backchannel ("mm-hm", keep going) and an interruption (stop talking).

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: sound while the other speaksbackchannel: keep goinginterruption: yield

Recall

Prompt Answer
Typical gap between turns in human talk ~200 ms (across ten languages, Stivers et al. 2009)
Why can't an agent just wait for silence? thinking pauses are silent too; waiting long enough to be safe is far slower than 200 ms
A backchannel is a listener signal ("mm-hm", "right") that is not a bid for the turn
An interruption is sustained speech over the agent: yield
Why do most agents not say "mm-hm" themselves? in a cascade it lands late and interrupts the person
Draw four timelines: pause, end, backchannel, interruption who is speaking, the silence, and what the agent should do in each

The idea

Without it: the agent treats every silence as "your turn" and every sound as "stop", so it cuts people off at thinking pauses and freezes at a cough.

It does: gives each sound a class and each class a response; endpointing handles pause vs end, barge-in handles backchannel vs interruption.

It costs: every classifier is wrong sometimes, in both directions; the tuning question is which error the product can afford.

How it works

What the person does Sounds like Agent should Stage that decides
Pauses to think mid-answer silence after "I think the answer is…" keep waiting endpoint (semantic turn detector)
Finishes silence after "…so I'd shard by tenant." reply endpoint
Backchannels while the agent speaks short "mm-hm", "yeah" keep speaking yield (interruption filter)
Interrupts sustained speech over the agent stop now; resume if no words follow yield (barge-in)

Knobs

Knob Default (as of Oct 2026) Raise it → Lower it →
Minimum silence before "finished" turn detector's own fewer cut-offs, slower replies snappier, more cut-offs
Minimum speech to count as an interruption LiveKit min_duration ignores "mm-hm" stops sooner on a real interruption
Interruption mode LiveKit adaptive on Cloud with most STT, else vad – –

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Thinking pauses 0.8 s minimum silence, up to 3.5 s when the model hears a mid-thought as_built §2 row 6; 0.5 s cut answers
Interruptions ≥ 0.4 s of voice stops Rachel; resume if no words in 2 s as_built §2 row 11
Agent backchannels off: responsiveness comes from latency, not filler sounds interview_prep/07 §4

Measure it

  • Metric — cut-off rate (agent spoke while the person was mid-answer) and false-interruption rate (agent stopped for a non-interruption).
  • See it — listen to recorded turns where the next user turn starts within ~1 s of the agent's reply: those are cut-offs.
  • Bounded by — resume after a false interruption; an apology line when a cut-off is detected.

Pitfalls

Targeting the human 200 ms gap

  • Why it's tempting: it's the natural number, so it looks like the right goal.
  • Why it's wrong: people hit it by predicting; an agent that waits only 200 ms of silence interrupts every thinker.
  • Think instead: aim for under a second end to end, and spend the wait where the model is unsure.

Treating every sound as an interruption

  • Why it's tempting: stopping fast feels polite.
  • Why it's wrong: "mm-hm" and coughs halt the agent mid-question; the person hears a broken sentence.
  • Think instead: require sustained speech, or words, before yielding; resume on a false alarm.

Connections

… → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield — the two decisions this note defines.

  • decided by endpointing and semantic turn detection (pause vs end).
  • decided by barge-in and backchannel handling (backchannel vs interruption).
  • sets the target in the latency budget.
  • handled by the model in full-duplex shapes.
  • Say it: Q6 · Q7

notes.title: The Voice Number Line
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_design.md App. B Twelve terms · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/as_built.md §3

TL;DR

Six numbers frame every voice design: the 20 ms frame, the ~200 ms human gap, the ~300 ms TTS first byte, the 800 ms p95 target, the ~1 s "feels natural" line, and the 3.4 s our build measures.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · design time

The idea

Number What it is Status
20 ms one audio frame; per-frame stages run 50×/s durable
~200 ms gap between turns in human talk (Stivers et al. 2009) durable
~300 ms TTS first byte we target; 342 ms p50 measured /
450 / 800 ms our p50 / p95 target, end of speech → first audio
~1 s LiveKit: conversations feel natural under about one second (as of Oct 2026) vendor
3 383 ms our p50, 30 days to 16 Oct 2026, callers in India

🔊 In our system

The gap between 800 ms and 3 383 ms is the endpoint wait and one model call: the latency budget.

Connections

puts in order the budget and human turn-taking.
